questionText: Under which designation was the EU AI Act published in the Official Journal?
explanation: A regulation applies directly in every Member State; a directive must first be transposed into national law.

questionText: Since when has Article 4 on AI literacy been applicable?
explanation: Art. 113 point (a) makes Art. 4 and the prohibitions in Art. 5 applicable from 2 February 2025; per the Commission FAQ, national supervision and enforcement of Art. 4 start on 2 August 2026. This does not automatically mean that the same fine applies to every infringement. (Source: claimId ai-literacy-supervision-2026-08-02)

questionText: A German SME uses Microsoft Copilot. Which role does it have under Art. 3?

answerOptions.text: Provider, because it uses AI in the organisation
Deployer, because it uses a finished AI system under its authority
Distributor, because it distributes Microsoft licences
Importer, because the AI comes from the United States

explanation: Under Art. 3(4), a deployer uses an AI system under its own authority, as SMEs almost always do. The provider is the producer, here Microsoft.

questionText: A US SaaS provider sells its AI platform to a company in Berlin. Does the EU AI Act apply to it?

answerOptions.text: No. US companies are outside its scope
Yes, Art. 2(1)(a) also covers providers from third countries

explanation: Art. 2(1)(a) applies because the provider places the platform on the EU market; under Art. 2(1)(c), EU use of the output would suffice. Location is irrelevant, and either trigger establishes the Regulation's applicability independently.

questionText: How many prohibited practices does Article 5 of the AI Act list?
explanation: Art. 5(1), points (a) to (h), lists eight, including social scoring, manipulative techniques, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces and emotion recognition at work.

questionText: An SME introduces an AI tool to screen job applications. Which risk class applies?

answerOptions.text: Minimal risk, because HR is not a critical area
Limited risk with a transparency obligation only

explanation: Annex III, point 4(a), classifies AI for recruiting or selecting people, such as evaluating applications, as high-risk. Every obligation in Chapter III, Section 2 then applies.

questionText: Which risk class applies to a conventional email spam filter under the EU AI Act?
explanation: Spam filters fall under neither Annex I nor Annex III and trigger no transparency obligation under Art. 50. Only voluntary codes of conduct under Art. 95 apply.

questionText: A company plans to use AI to infer employees' emotions during video calls. Is this permitted?

answerOptions.text: Yes, if the works council agrees
No. It is prohibited under Art. 5(1)(f)
Yes, as a high-risk system with a conformity assessment

explanation: Art. 5(1)(f) prohibits emotion recognition in workplaces and educational institutions, except for medical or safety reasons. Consent or works-council approval does not lift the prohibition.

questionText: What does Article 50 require for a publicly accessible chatbot on your website?

answerOptions.text: A conformity assessment by a notified body
A notice that users are interacting with an AI system
A report to the Federal Network Agency

explanation: Art. 50(1) requires providers to design chatbots so users are clearly informed they are interacting with AI, unless this is obvious. The notice must be clear, distinguishable and accessible.

questionText: What is the minimum retention period for the automatic logs of a high-risk AI system?
explanation: Art. 19(1) requires providers to keep them for at least 6 months, unless applicable Union or national law requires a longer period. Art. 26(6) sets the same for deployers.

questionText: Which Article sets the requirements for training, validation and testing data of high-risk AI?
explanation: Art. 10 requires data governance and data sets that are relevant, sufficiently representative and, as far as possible, error-free and complete. Art. 9 covers risk management, Art. 13 transparency towards deployers.

questionText: A high-risk system under Annex III, point 4 (applicant selection) is to be placed on the market. Which conformity-assessment route applies?

answerOptions.text: Only a notified body under Annex VII
Internal control under Annex VI (Art. 43(2)), without a notified body
Authorisation by the Federal Network Agency

explanation: Art. 43(2) requires internal control under Annex VI for Annex III, points 2 to 8; a notified body is not provided for here. Only biometrics under point 1 can fall under Annex VII if harmonised standards were not applied in full.

questionText: Which item does NOT belong in the technical documentation required by Annex IV?

answerOptions.text: A general description of the AI system and its intended purpose
A description of elements and development process
Information about monitoring, functioning and control

explanation: Annex IV lists nine categories, such as system description, development, monitoring, performance metrics, risk management and changes. Financial reports are not among them.

questionText: Which marking is mandatory before a high-risk AI system is placed on the market?
explanation: Art. 48 requires CE marking. It shows that the conformity assessment under Art. 43 is done and the EU declaration of conformity drawn up.

questionText: Above which cumulative amount of training compute is a GPAI model presumed to have systemic risk?
explanation: Art. 51(2) sets the threshold at 10^25 floating-point operations, and the Commission may adjust it by delegated act. Models in the GPT-4, Claude 3 and Gemini Ultra class are above it.

questionText: Article 4 establishes an organisational duty concerning AI literacy. To whom is that duty primarily addressed?

answerOptions.text: Providers and deployers of AI systems, as organisations
IT departments in organisations with more than 250 employees

explanation: Art. 4(1) requires providers and deployers to support AI literacy among staff and others acting on their behalf, considering the named context. Since Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, they do not have to guarantee that each person reaches a particular level of proficiency.

questionText: When did the European Commission publish the final version of the GPAI Code of Practice?
explanation: The AI Office published the Code on 10 July 2025. Signatories such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Mistral may use adherence as a means of demonstrating compliance (Art. 53(4), Art. 55(2)), but this does not create a presumption of conformity in the legal sense; only harmonised standards under Art. 40 and 41 would. (Source: AI Office, GPAI Code of Practice, 10 July 2025; Art. 53(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)

questionText: Which obligation do you have as a deployer when you use generative AI to write marketing copy for your website?

answerOptions.text: None; deployers have no transparency obligations
Disclosure under Art. 50(4) for public text on matters of public interest
Place CE marking on every page

explanation: Art. 50(4) requires disclosure of AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless the content has undergone human review or editorial control. Ordinary product marketing is covered only in limited cases.

questionText: What is the highest fine tier under Art. 99 for prohibited practices?

answerOptions.text: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of annual turnover
Up to EUR 15 million or 3% of annual turnover
Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover
Up to EUR 50 million or 10% of annual turnover

explanation: Art. 99(3) sets up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for infringements of Art. 5, whichever is higher. The other tiers are 3% and 1%.

questionText: Which authority does the KI-MIG, in force since 29 July 2026, designate as the single point of contact?

answerOptions.text: Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action

explanation: The KI-MIG, in force since 29 July 2026, makes the Federal Network Agency the market-surveillance authority, single point of contact and complaints body, unless a sectoral authority is responsible. Its official website sets out the complaints route.

questionText: Within what period must a provider report a serious incident under the general rule?

answerOptions.text: Immediately and no later than 24 hours
Immediately, no later than 15 days after becoming aware
Annually as part of post-market monitoring

explanation: Art. 73(2) requires reporting immediately and no later than 15 days after becoming aware. In the event of death the period is 10 days; for widespread infringements or critical infrastructure, 2 days.

questionText: Who may lodge a complaint about an alleged infringement of the AI Act under Art. 85?

answerOptions.text: Only through a lawyer with proof of authority

explanation: Art. 85 gives any natural or legal person the right to complain to the relevant market-surveillance authority, even without being directly affected. The authority decides how to proceed.

questionText: A private SME uses an AI CV-screening tool, high-risk under Annex III, point 4. Must it carry out a fundamental-rights impact assessment under Art. 27?

answerOptions.text: Yes, once it processes more than 100 applications per year
No, only public bodies and Annex III, points 5(b) and 5(c)
No, because CV screening is not a high-risk use

explanation: Art. 27(1) covers public bodies, private providers of public services and Annex III, points 5(b) and 5(c). A private HR use listed under point 4 is outside that scope. A DPIA under GDPR Art. 35 is separate, required only where the processing is likely to result in a high risk.

questionText: Which GDPR Article is the central bridge to risk work under the AI Act?

answerOptions.text: GDPR Art. 6 on lawfulness of processing
GDPR Art. 32 on security of processing
GDPR Art. 35 on data protection impact assessments
GDPR Art. 44 on transfers to third countries

explanation: AI Act Art. 26(9) expressly refers to the DPIA under GDPR Art. 35. Deployers can extend existing DPIAs with AI matters such as training data, human oversight and logging.

questionText: What is the first step in a five-step AI Act audit for an SME?

answerOptions.text: Build an inventory of every AI system in use
Perform a data protection impact assessment

explanation: Only an inventory with provider, purpose and data flows makes risk classification possible. Documentation, gap analysis and remediation follow.

questionText: You interact with a support chatbot. From when must the AI interaction generally be apparent under Art. 50(1)?

answerOptions.text: From 2 August 2026, before or at the start of the interaction
From 2 February 2025, if the chatbot system is registered
Only from 2 December 2027, when the high-risk rules apply
Only for chatbots with a GPAI licence

explanation: Providers must design systems that interact directly with people so that those people are told at the latest at the first interaction, unless this is obvious. The obligation applies from 2 August 2026. (Source: Art. 50(1), Art. 113 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)

questionText: Who is outside the scope of the AI Act when using AI solely for private purposes?

answerOptions.text: No one; the Regulation applies to every natural person
Natural persons using AI purely privately (Art. 2(10))
Only people in countries outside the EU

explanation: Art. 2(10) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 excludes deployer obligations for natural persons in a purely personal, non-professional activity. Using ChatGPT at home for your own writing is not covered; professional use is.
